title: 10. Security & Auth: Authentication
summary: Authentication is the process of verifying that an entity (user, service, or device) is who it claims to be, typically by checking one or more factors: something you know (password), something you have (token), or something…
objectives: What are the three authentication factors, and why does combining factors of different types matter?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Authentication is the process of verifying that an entity (user, service, or device) is who it claims to be, typically by checking one or more factors: something you know (password), something you have (token), or something you are (biometric).

Authentication answers a single question — "who are you?" — but the simplicity of the question hides enormous operational complexity. Every web service, every mobile app, every microservice that accepts an incoming request has to decide whether to trust the identity presented to it, and that decision determines what data leaks, what money moves, and what legal liability is incurred. The cost of getting authentication wrong is so high that, by 2024, Microsoft reported more than 4,000 identity-related attacks per second on its cloud — a number driven almost entirely by weak passwords, leaked credentials, and missing multi-factor authentication (MFA). Authentication is therefore not a "login form" feature; it is the security perimeter of every modern system, especially once perimeters dissolved behind cloud adoption and zero-trust networking.

The classical mental model for authentication is the three factors of identity, often called "something you know, something you have, something you are." A password is the canonical "something you know." A hardware key (YubiKey), a one-time password (OTP) on a phone, or a smartcard is "something you have." A fingerprint, face scan, or iris pattern is "something you are." Combining two of these yields two-factor authentication (2FA); combining more than one of the same type is "step-up" but not true multi-factor. The intuition is simple: a single factor can be compromised through one attack vector, but two factors of different types require an attacker to compromise two independent vectors simultaneously, which dramatically reduces risk. Google famously reported in 2018 that, after rolling out hardware security keys to all 85,000 employees, it had zero confirmed phishing-driven account takeovers for more than a year — a striking validation of strong-factor authentication at scale.

Passwords, despite being despised, remain the most common first factor. The engineering discipline around them has hardened over two decades. Modern password storage must use a slow, salted key-derivation function — bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2id — never MD5 or unsalted SHA. bcrypt's adjustable cost factor lets operators slow it down as hardware improves, ensuring that a leaked hash database still takes years per guess on commodity GPUs. The 2012 LinkedIn breach exposed 6.5 million unsalted SHA-1 hashes; in 2016 the same attackers sold 167 million records, including 117 million passwords cracked in days, illustrating precisely why salted slow hashes are mandatory. NIST 800-63B now also recommends banning commonly-used and previously-breached passwords (via services like HaveIBeenPwned's k-anonymity API), dropping periodic forced rotation (which pushes users toward weaker patterns like "Spring2024!"), and allowing long passphrases up to 64 characters or more.

MFA itself has a quality spectrum. SMS-based OTPs are technically MFA but are the weakest form: SIM-swap attacks, SS7 interception, and forwarding scams make SMS unreliable, and NIST deprecated SMS for new deployments in 2016. TOTP (RFC 6238) apps like Google Authenticator and Authy are stronger because they compute the OTP locally from a shared secret and the current 30-second time window, removing the telco from the trust chain. Push-based MFA (Microsoft Authenticator number matching, Duo Push) is stronger still because it resists phishing by requiring users to enter a number displayed on the login screen into the phone, defeating automated relay attacks. The strongest production deployments use FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware keys or platform authenticators (Touch ID, Windows Hello), which are phishing-resistant by design because the authenticator cryptographically binds to the origin (the domain) the user is signing into — a fake site cannot receive the credential even if the user is fooled.

Single sign-on (SSO) and passwordless authentication are the two directions mainstream enterprise security is moving. SSO lets a user authenticate once against an identity provider (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace) and access dozens of downstream apps via federation protocols like SAML or OpenID Connect. The benefit is fewer passwords to remember, faster deprovisioning when an employee leaves, and centralized MFA enforcement. The trade-off is the identity provider becomes a single point of failure: when Okta was breached in October 2023 and its support case management system was accessed, attackers potentially had a path to pivot into the 18,000+ downstream customer environments Okta federated. Passwordless authentication removes the password entirely, replacing it with a passkey (a FIDO2 credential synced across a user's devices via iCloud Keychain or Google Password Manager). Apple, Google, and Microsoft shipped passkey support between 2022 and 2023; by 2024 Google reported passkey adoption had reached over 400 million accounts, with sign-in success rates 4x higher and times 50% faster than passwords. The trade-off is recovery: a lost device with no synced backup can lock a user out permanently, so passwordless systems must invest heavily in account-recovery flows.

The fundamental trade-off in authentication design is security versus friction. Every additional factor adds 5–15 seconds to login and produces a measurable conversion drop in consumer products; every removed factor adds attack surface. Netflix, for example, deliberately avoids MFA on consumer accounts because the friction would cost subscriptions, even though this enables widespread credential-stuffing and account-sharing — instead they invest in device fingerprinting and anomaly detection on the back end. Google Workspace, AWS, and Azure AD force MFA on every user because the cost of a single admin account compromise is catastrophic. The right answer is risk-based authentication: step up to MFA when login is from a new device, new geography, or matches a known attack pattern, and let returning users on trusted devices sail through. This matches how Google's own account security works — a familiar laptop on home Wi-Fi logs in with just a password, while a new phone on a VPN is challenged for both an OTP and a hardware key. Authentication is therefore never a static decision; it is a continuous, risk-scored judgment the system re-evaluates on every request.

sections.title: Visual Explanation
sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant C as Client (Browser)
    participant IDP as Identity Provider
    participant TOTP as TOTP Authenticator App
    participant S as Backend Service

    U->>C: Enter username + password
    C->>IDP: POST /login (credentials)
    IDP->>IDP: Verify password hash (bcrypt)
    alt Password valid
        IDP->>U: Challenge: enter TOTP code
        U->>TOTP: Open app, read 6-digit code
        TOTP-->>U: 482913 (30s window)
        U->>C: Enter code
        C->>IDP: POST /login/verify (code)
        IDP->>IDP: Validate TOTP (HMAC-SHA1 + time)
        IDP-->>C: Issue session token / JWT
        C->>S: GET /api with token
        S-->>C: 200 OK (data)
    else Password invalid
        IDP-->>C: 401 (rate-limit after 5 tries)
    end
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
+----------+     1. user/pass     +-----------------+
|   User   | ------------------> |  Identity Prov. |
+----------+                     |  (auth server)  |
     ^                           +-----------------+
     | 2. MFA challenge                   |
     |                          +--------+--------+
     v                          |  bcrypt verify  |
+----------+   3. 6-digit OTP   |  TOTP verify    |
| TOTP App | <------------------+  risk scoring   |
| (mobile) | ------------------> +-----------------+
+----------+   4.OTP back                |
                                   5. issue JWT
                                        |
                                        v
                                +-----------------+
                                |  Session Store  |
                                |  / Refresh Tok. |
                                +-----------------+
                                        |
                                        v
+----------+   6. bearer token   +-----------------+
|  Client  | ------------------> |  Backend API    |
| (cookie) | <------------------ |  (verify JWT)   |
+----------+      200 OK         +-----------------+
```

### Walkthrough
1. The user submits credentials; the identity provider looks up the stored bcrypt hash and verifies it with constant-time comparison. Failure triggers rate limiting; five failures lock the account for 15 minutes.
2. The provider issues a second-factor challenge — typically a TOTP code generated from a shared secret and a 30-second time window — and waits for the client to return it.
3. The provider validates the OTP, computes a risk score (new device? new ASN? impossible-travel?), and if all checks pass, mints a short-lived JWT plus a long-lived refresh token stored against the user's session.
4. The client uses the JWT as a bearer token on every API call; the backend verifies signature, expiry, and scopes before authorizing the request.
5. When the JWT expires, the client silently exchanges the refresh token for a new JWT; if the refresh token is rotated and the old one reappears, the provider revokes the entire session family (token theft detection).

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
# Authentication mock: bcrypt-style password hashing + TOTP-style MFA.
# NOT production crypto — illustrative only.
import hashlib, hmac, time, base64, json, secrets

# --- 1. Password hashing (simplified bcrypt-like: salt + PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256) ---
def hash_password(password: str, cost: int = 100_000) -> str:
    salt = secrets.token_bytes(16)                        # 128-bit salt
    dk = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", password.encode(),
                             salt, cost)
    # store as "pbkdf2$cost$salt_hex$hash_hex"
    return f"pbkdf2${cost}${salt.hex()}${dk.hex()}"

def verify_password(password: str, stored: str) -> bool:
    algo, cost, salt_hex, hash_hex = stored.split("$")
    dk = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", password.encode(),
                             bytes.fromhex(salt_hex), int(cost))
    return hmac.compare_digest(dk.hex(), hash_hex)

# --- 2. TOTP-style MFA (RFC 6238 simplified) ---
def totp_now(secret: bytes, window: int = 30, digits: int = 6) -> str:
    counter = int(time.time() // window)
    msg = counter.to_bytes(8, "big")
    hs = hmac.new(secret, msg, hashlib.sha1).digest()
    offset = hs[-1] & 0x0F
    binary = ((hs[offset] & 0x7F) << 24 |
              (hs[offset+1] & 0xFF) << 16 |
              (hs[offset+2] & 0xFF) << 8 |
              (hs[offset+3] & 0xFF))
    return str(binary % (10 ** digits)).zfill(digits)

def totp_verify(secret: bytes, code: str, skew: int = 1) -> bool:
    # allow current window +/- skew to absorb clock drift
    for delta in range(-skew, skew + 1):
        if totp_at(secret, int(time.time()) + delta * 30) == code:
            return True
    return False

def totp_at(secret: bytes, ts: int) -> str:
    counter = ts // 30
    msg = counter.to_bytes(8, "big")
    hs = hmac.new(secret, msg, hashlib.sha1).digest()
    offset = hs[-1] & 0x0F
    binary = ((hs[offset] & 0x7F) << 24 |
              (hs[offset+1] & 0xFF) << 16 |
              (hs[offset+2] & 0xFF) << 8 |
              (hs[offset+3] & 0xFF))
    digits = 6
    return str(binary % (10 ** digits)).zfill(digits)

# --- 3. Login flow ---
USERS = {"alice": hash_password("correct horse battery staple")}
MFA_SECRET = secrets.token_bytes(20)              # shared at enrollment

def login(username: str, password: str, otp: str) -> str | None:
    if username not in USERS:
        return None
    if not verify_password(password, USERS[username]):
        return None
    if not totp_verify(MFA_SECRET, otp):
        return None
    # success: issue a mock session token
    return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(
        json.dumps({"u": username, "iat": int(time.time())}).encode()
    ).decode()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    code = totp_now(MFA_SECRET)
    token = login("alice", "correct horse battery staple", code)
    print("Logged in, token:", token[:24] + "..." if token else "FAILED")
```

quiz.question: What are the three authentication factors, and why does combining factors of different types matter?
options: Authentication answers "who are you?" and verifies identity; authorization answers "what are you allowed to do?" and grants or denies specific actions on specific resources.
The benefits are operational: users memorize one strong password instead of fifty weak ones, MFA is enforced centrally, joining and leaving employees are deprovisioned in one place, and…
The trade-offs are recovery and portability: if a user loses their only device without a synced backup, they can be permanently locked out; if the sync provider is breached, all synced…
The three classical factors are something you know (password, PIN), something you have (hardware key, OTP app on phone, smartcard), and something you are (fingerprint, face, iris, voice).
quiz.explanation: The three classical factors are something you know (password, PIN), something you have (hardware key, OTP app on phone, smartcard), and something you are (fingerprint, face, iris, voice). Multi-factor authentication is only effective when the factors come from different categories, because an attacker has to compromise two independent mechanisms. Two passwords are not MFA — a single phishing site steals both.

If the score is low (a returning user on a known device at the usual home ASN), the system allows password-only login to preserve conversion.
